paragraphs: Evaluating an agent only by its final output can miss important parts of how it solved a task. Examining the full process manually, however, requires substantial work. Agent-as-a-Judge addresses this problem by using an agentic system as the evaluator, extending language-model judging with capabilities for assessing intermediate steps and providing feedback throughout task execution.

The paper tests this approach on code generation and introduces DevAI as a supporting benchmark. DevAI contains 55 realistic AI coding tasks with detailed manual annotations, including 365 solution requirements organized hierarchically. These requirements give the evaluator a structured basis for assessing whether a solution meets its different obligations, rather than treating completion as one undifferentiated outcome.

The authors evaluate three leading code-generating agent systems. In this setting, Agent-as-a-Judge substantially outperforms LLM-as-a-Judge and matches the reliability of the human evaluation baseline. The findings support process-aware automated evaluation for these coding tasks and provide a concrete testbed for developing more capable agent evaluators.
icml-2025-agent-as-a-judge-evaluate-agen.tldr: Agent-as-a-Judge evaluates agents’ intermediate work and matches a human evaluation baseline on a new AI coding benchmark.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to discover formula-based financial signals that work well together. It treats this search as a sequence of decisions, modeled as a Markov decision process with changing conditions and sparse rewards. This framing makes both challenges explicit: feedback is infrequent, and the search cannot assume that its reward environment remains fixed.

AlphaQCM addresses these challenges through distributional reinforcement learning. One network learns the Q function, which evaluates decisions, while another learns quantiles describing the reward distribution. A quantiled conditional moment method then uses those potentially biased quantile estimates to learn unbiased variance. The resulting search is guided by both learned value and variance, rather than relying on the Q function alone.

Applications to real-world datasets show that AlphaQCM significantly outperforms its competitors, especially on large datasets containing many stocks. The stated finding concerns the effectiveness of discovering complementary formulaic alphas. Its methodological contribution is to connect sequential search with distributional information that helps navigate sparse feedback and non-stationarity.
icml-2025-alphaqcm-alpha-discovery-in-fi.tldr: AlphaQCM uses learned values and reward variance to search efficiently for complementary financial signals under changing conditions and sparse feedback.

paragraphs: Safe online reinforcement learning must pursue rewards while respecting constraints on its behavior. The paper considers a particularly demanding version of this problem: constraints are initially unknown, change over time, and may be chosen adversarially. Methods designed around stochastic constraints can fail in this setting, motivating an algorithm that explicitly accounts for adversarial changes.

The proposed Optimistic Mirror Descent Primal-Dual algorithm, OMDPD, addresses constrained Markov decision processes with anytime adversarial constraints. It achieves an optimal regret bound and a strong constraint-violation bound that both scale with the square root of K, up to logarithmic factors. These bounds describe how reward shortfall and constraint violations accumulate; they do not assert that violations never occur.

The guarantees do not require Slater’s condition or advance knowledge of a strictly safe policy. The paper also shows that accurate reward and transition estimates can improve the bounds further. Together, these results establish controlled learning performance under adversarial constraints while reducing reliance on safety assumptions required by other approaches.
icml-2025-an-optimistic-algorithm-for-on.tldr: OMDPD bounds regret and constraint violations under adversarially changing constraints without requiring a known strictly safe policy.

paragraphs: Best subset selection seeks a useful collection of features, and many algorithms build that collection by repeatedly adding or removing features. This paper revisits the rules used to make those decisions. Its central observation is that classical selection and elimination criteria account for only part of the change in the optimization objective after a feature enters or leaves.

The authors formulate optimization subproblems for feature entry and exit and solve them exactly. These solutions produce two replacement criteria, one for adding features and another for removing them. The resulting decisions are proved optimal for the current entry or exit process. This is a statement about each decision within that process, rather than a claim that every complete subset search reaches a global optimum.

Replacing existing criteria yields enhanced versions of multiple subset-selection algorithms while preserving their theoretical properties. Across tasks including compressed sensing and sparse regression, the paper reports substantial gains across different evaluation measures without increasing computational cost. The contribution therefore improves a shared decision mechanism used by several algorithms.
icml-2025-best-subset-selection-optimal-.tldr: Exact feature-entry and feature-exit criteria improve existing subset-selection algorithms without increasing their computational cost.

paragraphs: Low-rank adaptation adjusts large foundation models through adapters, but their optimization can become trapped near initialization in suboptimal solutions. The paper connects this problem to weaker generalization and difficulties with later operations such as merging adapters or pruning them. CoTo changes the training schedule to encourage adapters to explore a broader range of solutions.

During fine-tuning, CoTo randomly deactivates adapters and gradually increases their probability of being active. This progressive participation is intended to balance optimization across adapters. The theoretical analysis shows that the strategy promotes layer-wise dropout stability and linear mode connectivity. The authors also use a cooperative-game approach to quantify each adapter’s marginal contribution, connecting individual adapters to their contribution within the combined system.

Experiments report consistent improvements in single-task performance, multi-task merging accuracy, and robustness to pruning, together with reduced training overhead. CoTo also works with diverse LoRA variants. These findings suggest that changing when adapters participate can improve both their immediate performance and their usefulness in subsequent model-combination or simplification steps.
icml-2025-come-together-but-not-right-no.tldr: CoTo gradually activates LoRA adapters during training, improving task performance, merging, and pruning while reducing training overhead.

paragraphs: Directed graphs contain relationships whose behavior depends on direction. A path from one node to another can differ substantially from the return path. The paper argues that conventional graph neural networks capture one-way relations more readily than these mutual path dependencies, leaving useful information about asymmetric connectivity underrepresented during learning.

Commute Graph Neural Networks address this gap by incorporating node-wise commute time into message passing. The method introduces a directed-graph Laplacian that supports efficient commute-time computation. At each layer, the network weights neighboring nodes’ contributions according to their commute time to the central node. This makes the aggregation process sensitive to mutual connectivity rather than relying only on the presence of directed neighboring relationships.

Experiments across eight benchmark datasets show better performance than thirteen state-of-the-art methods. The reported results support using commute-time information as part of graph learning on directed structures. The distinctive contribution is the combination of an efficient structural calculation with a direct role for that calculation in every layer’s neighborhood aggregation.
icml-2025-commute-graph-neural-networks-.tldr: Commute Graph Neural Networks use commute-time-weighted message passing to capture mutual path relationships in directed graphs.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional occupancy prediction describes a scene through small spatial cells, or voxels, allowing finer obstacle contours than bounding boxes. CSV-Occ addresses two problems in image-based occupancy prediction: combining information over time can be computationally expensive, and semantic ambiguity can cause the interiors of foreground objects to be incorrectly labeled as empty.

For temporal processing, the method extends a state space model to handle interactions among multiple input sequences. A cascaded architecture reduces the stated temporal-modeling complexity from quadratic to linear. For object interiors, voxels explicitly vote for the center of their instance. The model then learns to use features from other voxels belonging to that instance to refine internal gaps from coarse to fine.

CSV-Occ achieves state-of-the-art camera-based occupancy prediction on Occ3D-nuScenes and also performs well on nuScenes lidar semantic segmentation. These results support the combination of more efficient temporal fusion and instance-based semantic refinement. The two components address different obstacles to useful scene representations: processing cost and incorrect empty regions inside objects.
icml-2025-csv-occ-fusing-multi-frame-ali.tldr: CSV-Occ combines linear-complexity temporal modeling with object-center voting to improve three-dimensional occupancy predictions.

paragraphs: Multiplayer optimization requires players to update their strategies while accounting for what other players are doing. Frequent strategy exchanges can become a substantial communication burden. Decoupled SGDA adapts stochastic gradient descent ascent so that players can continue making local updates using outdated information about opponents, allowing computation to proceed between communication events.

The paper analyzes this approach for strongly convex–strongly concave games. In that setting, it achieves near-optimal communication complexity comparable to the best-known gradient descent ascent rates. It also identifies a favorable regime of weak coupling, where interactions between players are smaller relative to the parts of the game that do not depend on other players.

For these weakly coupled games, Decoupled SGDA significantly reduces communication costs compared with standard SGDA. The paper additionally reports better performance than federated minimax approaches in noisy, imbalanced settings. The contribution is a way to separate local strategy improvement from frequent information exchange, with the strongest stated communication advantages tied to the game’s interaction structure.
icml-2025-decoupled-sgda-for-games-with-.tldr: Decoupled SGDA lets players update using stale opponent strategies, reducing communication especially in weakly coupled games.

paragraphs: LiDAR point clouds contain reflectance attributes that matter for downstream tasks, yet these attributes have received limited attention in neural compression. SerLiC focuses on their structure from the sensor’s perspective. It first arranges three-dimensional points into a one-dimensional sequence following scan order, giving the compression model an ordering connected to how the measurements were acquired.

Each point receives a contextual representation containing its scanning index, radial distance, and prior reflectance. These inputs support modeling dependencies along the sequence. SerLiC uses Mamba with a dual parallelization scheme to combine autoregressive dependency modeling with fast processing, addressing the tension between exploiting sequential information and maintaining efficient computation.

Experiments report more than a twofold reduction in reflectance-data volume. Compared with the state-of-the-art method, SerLiC uses only 2% as many parameters and reduces compressed bits by up to 22%. A lightweight version reaches at least ten frames per second with 111,000 parameters. These findings support scan-order modeling as an effective and compact approach to reflectance compression.
icml-2025-efficient-lidar-reflectance-co.tldr: SerLiC compresses LiDAR reflectance by modeling scan-ordered sequences, achieving strong compression with a small parameter count.

paragraphs: External control data can supplement randomized trials when recruiting a large randomized sample is difficult or unethical. However, historical or observational controls may differ systematically from trial participants. The paper addresses the risk that borrowing such data inflates false-positive rates, particularly in small trials where additional controls could be especially valuable.

The proposed framework bases inference on the trial’s randomization, providing finite-sample exact, model-free control of type I error. To improve statistical power, it uses conformal inference to assess external controls individually and selectively pool comparable ones. Crucially, the randomization tests account for uncertainty introduced by this selection, preserving valid inference after the borrowing decision.

An adaptive procedure chooses the selection threshold by minimizing mean squared error across estimators spanning no borrowing through full borrowing. Non-asymptotic theory, simulations, and an application combining a randomized lung cancer trial with National Cancer Database controls support the approach. The contribution links selective data use with explicit error control instead of treating external-control selection as a fixed preprocessing choice.
icml-2025-enhancing-statistical-validity.tldr: Randomization inference with conformal selection borrows comparable external controls while preserving finite-sample type I error control.

paragraphs: Standard regression losses compare each prediction with its own target. Other methods also compare pairs of examples in a learned feature space, but these comparisons can add computational expense. Gradient Aligned Regression, or GAR, instead introduces pairwise relationships directly in label space, combining an ordinary regression loss with two losses based on label differences.

The pairwise terms target gradient alignment in both magnitude and direction. The paper supplies a theoretical connection between learning differences in labels and learning the gradient of the underlying target function. Although pairwise comparisons initially suggest quadratic complexity, the proposed losses can be reduced to linear complexity, giving GAR efficiency at the same level as conventional regression losses.

The study explicitly limits its scope to clean data without noise, outliers, or distribution shifts. Within that setting, evaluations cover two synthetic datasets and eight real-world tasks from six benchmarks, with eight competing baselines. Runtime comparisons favor GAR over feature-space pairwise methods, while ablations support the contribution of each component.
icml-2025-gradient-aligned-regression-vi.tldr: GAR adds efficient pairwise label-difference losses to regression, connecting prediction training with gradient alignment in clean-data settings.

paragraphs: Multiple instance learning predicts from a collection of instances using weak supervision. In whole-slide histology, very large images commonly require a two-stage workflow: a pretrained backbone extracts features, and a separate aggregation model learns from them. The paper identifies noisy backbone features and weak supervision as obstacles to learning representations that generalize well.

The authors empirically investigate dropout in this setting. Their central observation is that removing the top-k most important instances from a bag can improve performance and generalization, including under a noise attack. This motivates MIL-Dropout, a method designed specifically for multiple instance learning that systematically chooses which instances to discard.

Experiments on five multiple-instance benchmarks and two whole-slide image datasets show improvements to existing MIL methods with negligible computational cost. The findings indicate that the selection of dropped instances matters: deliberately removing highly influential instances can be useful during training. The paper turns that empirical observation into a targeted dropout procedure for the aggregation stage.
icml-2025-how-effective-can-dropout-be-i.tldr: MIL-Dropout improves multiple instance learning by systematically dropping influential instances, with negligible computational cost.

paragraphs: Language models can struggle to retrieve the key information already present in their input. Mask-Enhanced Autoregressive Prediction, or MEAP, addresses this through a small training change: it randomly masks a fraction of input tokens and then applies ordinary autoregressive next-token prediction. The model remains a decoder-only Transformer.

This approach incorporates masking into next-token training without requiring bidirectional attention or an encoder-decoder architecture. The paper reports no additional computational overhead during pretraining or inference. Its analysis attributes the improvement to more distinguishable attention scores: concentrating attention on fewer visible tokens helps emphasize relevant signals and reduce the influence of peripheral context.

Experiments show substantial improvements over next-token prediction on information retrieval and long-context reasoning, with comparable or better commonsense reasoning. Benefits also appear during supervised fine-tuning, including a reported 11.77-percentage-point advantage in lost-in-the-middle scenarios. The findings suggest that selectively hiding input during training can improve how a model uses available context, despite leaving the basic prediction procedure intact.
icml-2025-mask-enhanced-autoregressive-p.tldr: MEAP masks a small fraction of training inputs to improve contextual retrieval and reasoning without additional computational overhead.

paragraphs: Language models increasingly generate datasets for tasks such as classification and summarization, but assessing how diverse those datasets are remains difficult. This paper introduces DCScore, which approaches diversity measurement through classification. It formulates evaluation as a sample classification task and uses relationships among samples, making their mutual structure central to the resulting score.

The authors provide theoretical verification that DCScore satisfies diversity-related axioms. This supplies a principled basis for the measure beyond its observed behavior on particular datasets. The contribution is therefore both a proposed calculation and an analysis of properties that support interpreting that calculation as a diversity measure.

Experiments on synthetic datasets find stronger correlations with several diversity pseudo-truths, which serve as reference signals for evaluating diversity. These are empirical comparisons against such proxies, rather than proof of agreement with a uniquely observable true diversity. Both theoretical and empirical results also show substantially lower computational costs than existing methods, supporting the method’s usefulness when diversity evaluation itself becomes expensive.
icml-2025-measuring-diversity-in-synthet.tldr: DCScore measures synthetic-data diversity through sample classification, combining theoretical properties with stronger proxy agreement and lower computational cost.

paragraphs: Indirect prompt injection occurs when malicious instructions inside tool-retrieved information redirect an agent toward unauthorized actions. MELON builds on a behavioral observation: during a successful attack, the agent’s next action becomes less dependent on the user’s task and more dependent on the malicious task embedded in the retrieved material.

The defense re-executes the agent’s trajectory after applying a masking function to the user prompt. It compares actions from the original and masked executions and flags an attack when those actions are similar. The comparison tests whether the next action remains largely unchanged despite altering the legitimate task. Three additional design elements aim to reduce false positives and false negatives.

On the AgentDojo benchmark, MELON outperforms state-of-the-art defenses in both attack prevention and preservation of normal utility. Combining it with a prompt-augmentation defense produces further improvements, and ablations examine its key design choices. The reported evidence supports task-dependence testing as a useful defense signal while explicitly recognizing the importance of avoiding mistaken detections.
icml-2025-melon-provable-defense-against.tldr: MELON detects indirect prompt injection by comparing agent actions before and after masking the legitimate user task.

paragraphs: Medical vision-language models can generate statements that conflict with an image when textual knowledge outweighs visual evidence. The paper argues that existing preference-optimization approaches inadequately account for clinical relevance, creating examples that are too easy to distinguish. MMedPO constructs preference data intended to address medically meaningful alignment failures.

The method introduces two kinds of undesirable examples. One contains plausible but medically inaccurate responses generated using the target model or GPT-4o. The other adds noise locally to lesion regions, disrupting the visual information in critical areas. Scores from multiple medical language models and visual tools then determine each sample’s clinical relevance for preference optimization.

Experiments show improved factual accuracy over existing preference-optimization methods, with reported improvements of 14.2% on medical visual question answering and 51.7% on report generation. These findings support the value of choosing clinically relevant preference examples rather than relying only on easily separated responses. The approach connects response accuracy with attention to the image regions that matter for the medical task.
icml-2025-mmedpo-aligning-medical-vision.tldr: MMedPO uses clinically relevant response errors and lesion-region corruption to improve medical vision-language models’ factual accuracy.

paragraphs: Brains differ substantially in structure and physiology, yet their neural circuits can support consistent functions across individuals. Earlier work found preserved motor-cortex representations after manual alignment between subjects. This paper examines whether such preservation can be validated zero-shot and whether it extends to additional cortical regions.

Probabilistic Neural-Behavioral Representation Alignment, or PNBA, models variation across trials, sessions, and subjects. It aligns neural and behavioral representations while applying generative constraints to prevent the learned representations from degenerating. This combination allows the framework to account for several levels of variability while maintaining useful structure in the aligned representations.

Using zero-shot validation, the authors find robust preserved representations in monkey primary motor and dorsal premotor cortices. They also establish similar preservation in mouse primary visual cortex. The findings provide evidence across the tested cortices and species that functional representations can remain consistent despite biological heterogeneity. The framework additionally enables zero-shot behavior decoding, connecting representational alignment with the ability to infer behavior from neural activity.
icml-2025-neural-representational-consis.tldr: PNBA probabilistically aligns neural and behavioral representations, revealing zero-shot representational preservation in tested monkey and mouse cortices.

paragraphs: Autoregressive models for time-dependent partial differential equations predict successive states, but errors can accumulate over long trajectories. The paper links this to a shortcut problem in autoregressive prediction. Under distribution shifts, the problem can become severe enough that pretrained models approach randomly initialized models in performance on downstream tasks involving long-term dynamics.

Physics-informed temporal alignment, or PITA, introduces self-supervised training inspired by inverse problem solving. For each observed trajectory, it aligns the physical dynamics discovered at different times. Physics-informed constraints become part of the learning signal, encouraging consistency in the dynamics represented across the trajectory rather than relying solely on successive prediction.

The alignment is derived from observations without requiring known physics priors. This is central to the method’s intended usefulness beyond the pretraining distribution. Across diverse time-dependent PDE datasets, experiments report significant gains in the accuracy and robustness of existing foundation models. The contribution is a data-derived temporal consistency signal designed to address the accumulation of errors during repeated prediction.
icml-2025-physics-informed-temporal-alig.tldr: PITA improves autoregressive PDE models by aligning dynamics across time using observation-derived physical constraints.

paragraphs: PieClam represents graph nodes in a code space and learns those representations by maximizing the likelihood of the reconstructed graph. It builds on community-affiliation approaches, but broadens what a community can express. Inclusive communities describe groups with strong connectivity, while exclusive communities describe groups characterized by strong disconnection.

The method also learns a prior over how nodes are distributed in the code space. This extends the model beyond a decoder based only on pairwise interactions and makes it a graph generative model. Together, the prior and the two kinds of communities provide a richer representation of graph structure, incorporating both patterns of connection and patterns of separation.

The authors introduce a similarity measure called log cut distance and use it to prove universal approximate reconstruction of graphs. That universality is expressed through the proposed measure. On graph anomaly detection and link prediction benchmarks, PieClam achieves competitive performance. The paper therefore combines a representational guarantee with empirical evidence on two graph-analysis tasks.
icml-2025-pieclam-a-universal-graph-auto.tldr: PieClam combines connected and disconnected communities with a learned prior, enabling universal approximate graph reconstruction under log cut distance.

paragraphs: Transformers use both token content and position to decide where to retrieve information. The paper argues that many positional encodings impose rigid attention patterns and learn general biases that do not adapt sufficiently to individual sequences. These restrictions can hinder long-range dependencies and specialization across different tasks.

TAPE makes positional encodings depend on sequence content across layers. Its dynamic positional representations can adapt to the current input, while permutation and orthogonal equivariance provide stability during updates. The paper also gives a theoretical result showing that TAPE can facilitate reasoning by allowing models to emulate a broader class of algorithms.

The framework integrates into pretrained transformers through parameter-efficient fine-tuning with minimal overhead. Experiments report better performance than existing positional embedding techniques on language modeling, arithmetic reasoning, and long-context retrieval. The theoretical and empirical contributions address complementary questions: what algorithmic behaviors the encoding can support, and whether its adaptive positional information improves performance on the evaluated tasks.
icml-2025-rethinking-addressing-in-langu.tldr: TAPE makes positional encodings content-aware and equivariant, improving evaluated reasoning, language modeling, and long-context retrieval tasks.

paragraphs: Uplift models aim to identify people likely to respond to a treatment, but evaluating their rankings is difficult because counterfactual outcomes are unavailable. This paper identifies a specific problem with uplift and Qini curves: they do not accurately rank individuals with negative binary outcomes. Consequently, a biased model can receive a better evaluation than an unbiased one.

The proposed Principled Uplift Curve, or PUC, addresses this imbalance by assigning equal curve values across positive and negative binary outcomes. The aim is to make evaluation more balanced instead of allowing one outcome category to distort model comparisons. The authors then derive a Principled Uplift Loss from the curve and incorporate it into PTONet, a treatment-and-outcome network.

Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets show less biased evaluation with PUC and better performance from PTONet than existing methods. The paper connects evaluation and training: correcting how rankings are assessed also supplies a learning objective intended to reduce bias while the model is being fitted.
icml-2025-rethinking-causal-ranking-a-ba.tldr: PUC balances uplift evaluation across binary outcomes and supplies a training loss that improves the proposed PTONet model.

paragraphs: Diffusion policies learn robot manipulation behavior from human demonstrations, but can struggle when objects appear in unfamiliar three-dimensional arrangements. Spherical Diffusion Policy addresses this by building in SE(3) equivariance: when the scene undergoes a three-dimensional rigid transformation, the generated trajectory adapts consistently with that transformation.

The method embeds states, actions, and the denoising process in spherical Fourier space. Spherical FiLM layers condition action denoising on scene representations while preserving equivariance. A spherical temporal U-net supplies an efficient denoising architecture with spatiotemporal equivariance. These components work together so that the transformation property applies end to end, covering both scene conditioning and action generation.

The paper reports large improvements over strong baselines on twenty simulation tasks and five physical robot tasks, including single-arm and two-arm embodiments. These results support the practical value of encoding the desired geometric behavior directly in the policy. The stated generalization benefit concerns transformed three-dimensional scenes, where the model’s equivariant structure provides a consistent relationship between observations and trajectories.
icml-2025-se-3-equivariant-diffusion-pol.tldr: Spherical Diffusion Policy builds three-dimensional transformation equivariance into robot action generation, improving performance across simulated and physical tasks.

paragraphs: Soft Reasoning addresses two obstacles in language-model reasoning: limited diversity among candidate solutions and inefficient search. It guides generation by optimizing the embedding of the first token. This makes the initial embedding the object of search, using changes in that representation to steer the solutions subsequently produced by the model.

The framework combines controlled embedding perturbations with Bayesian optimization. Perturbations provide exploration, while a verifier-guided objective directs refinement toward promising embeddings. Bayesian optimization balances exploring alternatives with exploiting candidates that already look useful. The verifier therefore has a direct role in shaping the search, connecting candidate generation with feedback about solution quality.

The paper reports improvements in reasoning accuracy and coherence, with experiments showing superior correctness using minimal computation. It presents the approach as scalable and model-agnostic. The central contribution is a controlled search procedure in embedding space that uses explicit verification feedback, offering a way to improve generation without relying on heuristic search to navigate the solution space.
icml-2025-soft-reasoning-navigating-solu.tldr: Soft Reasoning uses verifier-guided Bayesian optimization of the first token’s embedding to improve reasoning search and correctness.

paragraphs: Spatial transcriptomics records gene expression together with spatial coordinates, producing measurements that are discrete in space and extremely high-dimensional. SUICA models these data through a compact, continuous implicit neural representation. The goal is to enhance spatial density and gene-expression representation while accounting for the structure of the observed sampling locations.

A graph-augmented autoencoder captures contextual information among unstructured spots and produces structure-aware embeddings for spatial mapping. To handle the highly skewed expression distribution, SUICA treats regression through a classification-based formulation and uses classification losses during optimization. These components address different aspects of the problem: spatial relationships among measurements and the uneven distribution of expression values.

Across common spatial transcriptomics platforms and varying degradations, experiments show better numerical fidelity, statistical correlation, and biological conservation than conventional implicit representations and state-of-the-art methods. The predictions also amplify gene signatures in ways reported to enrich biological conservation and help subsequent analysis. The findings support combining spatial structure with distribution-aware learning for continuous representations of these data.
icml-2025-suica-learning-super-high-dime.tldr: SUICA combines graph-aware embeddings and classification-based learning to create compact, continuous representations of spatial gene-expression data.

paragraphs: Low-rank adaptation reduces the cost of adapting diffusion models, but using one adapter across all diffusion timesteps limits its ability to handle different noise levels. TimeStep Master addresses this with a two-stage training approach. It first trains separate LoRA experts over different timestep intervals so that they specialize in different portions of the diffusion process.

The second stage combines experts across multiple interval scales. For each timestep, the expert covering the smallest interval acts as an ungated core. Experts covering larger intervals provide context through time-dependent gates. This asymmetric arrangement preserves a fine-grained specialist while allowing broader-scale information to contribute adaptively to the model’s behavior.

Experiments cover domain adaptation, post-pretraining, and model distillation. The paper reports state-of-the-art results across these tasks using UNet, DiT, and MM-DiT architectures with image and video data. The findings support timestep specialization as a broadly useful adaptation strategy in the tested settings, with the expert mixture joining local noise-level modeling and wider temporal context.
icml-2025-timestep-master-asymmetrical-m.tldr: TimeStep Master combines LoRA experts specialized at different timestep scales to improve diffusion-model adaptation across image and video tasks.
